extracted.intended_audience: policy advocates, journalists, regulators, and members of the public concerned with rulemaking integrity and net neutrality
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and procedural expectations for maintaining the integrity of federal notice-and-comment rulemaking (with a focus on the FCC Net Neutrality proceeding), including detection of fraudulent comments, agency transparency, investigative cooperation, and remedial actions. The guidance is aimed at ensuring public input is authentic, accurately counted, and traceable to sponsors or funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of public comments / no fake comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments must be authentic and submitted by real individuals or authorized representatives; large numbers of faked comments corrupt the rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents that 'the submission of enormous numbers of faked comments is corrupting the process' and cites examples (names used without permission, comments in the names of dead people). Anti-pattern: accepting bulk, unauthenticated submissions without verification. Remedy: detect and exclude fraudulent submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency cooperation with investigators and law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should assist reporters, technologists, investigators, state attorneys general, and law enforcement in determining who is behind suspicious comment submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated calls in the timeline urge the FCC to help investigators; e.g., the New York AG asked the FCC to turn over logs and the AG 'urges Pai’s FCC to reconsider its refusal to assist law enforcement.' The page treats refusal to assist as an obstruction to accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and provision of comment logs (FOIA responsiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must produce comprehensive data logs and records related to comment submissions on request (including FOIA requests), enabling verification of how comments were submitted and by whom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The timeline notes Jason Prechtel 'sues the FCC for refusing to respond to a Freedom of Information Act request seeking comprehensive data logs' and the NY AG repeatedly requested logs. Guidance: timely disclosure of submission metadata is necessary for public trust and investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards to prevent comment-stuffing and large-scale fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should have procedures and technical safeguards in place to prevent large-scale automated or orchestrated comment-stuffing campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House Democrats asked GAO to 'determine what sorts of safeguards the FCC has in place to prevent this level of fraud.' Anti-pattern: no technical, procedural, or policy measures to detect bulk/fake submissions prior to counting them in the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay of final rulemaking actions pending investigation of fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should delay votes or final decisions when credible evidence of comment fraud exists until investigations can assess the integrity of the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts that '28 senators and Democratic FCC Commissioner Jessica Rosenworcel urge the FCC to delay its Net Neutrality vote to give investigators more time to look into the comment fraud' — the FCC did not delay. Guidance: postponement can be necessary to ensure decisions are based on a trustworthy record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation and subpoena of organizations and sponsors behind comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators should use subpoena power and other tools to identify groups, lead generators, and sponsors responsible for orchestrating or funding mass comment campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the New York attorney general subpoenas 14 organizations...to determine who was behind the submission of more than nine million fraudulent public comments.' Guidance: follow the money and organizational links to determine responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove duplicates and fake comments; analyze/count unique submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before drawing conclusions from a docket, agencies (or researchers) should remove duplicate and fake comments and base analyses on unique, verified submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanford researcher Ryan Singel 'after removing all duplicate and fake comments... finds that 99.7 percent of unique public comments favored keeping the Net Neutrality protections.' Guidance: counting unique comments (not raw totals) is necessary for an accurate picture of public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-decision transparency and assistance for public understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: If fraud is suspected or discovered, agencies should help the public, journalists, and policymakers understand what authentic public input actually said, even after decisions are finalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singel criticized the FCC: 'The FCC did nothing to try to prevent comment stuffing... and even after the vote, made no attempt to help the public, journalists, [and] policy makers actually understand what Americans actually told the FCC.' Guidance: agencies should proactively clarify the record and provide cleaned datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of sponsors, funders, and who 'sponsored' comment solicitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns soliciting comments should disclose the true sponsors and funders; use of intermediary 'sponsors' to mask industry involvement is improper and obscures accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NY AG report states Broadband for America 'recruited advocacy groups to 'sponsor' these comment solicitations to give the false impression' of diverse voices, thereby 'obscur[ing] the broadband industry's role.' Guidance: require sponsorship/funder disclosure for mass solicitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability, penalties, and required reforms for lead generators and firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies that generate fraudulent comments or assist in creating fraudulent mass comment campaigns should face penalties and be required to adopt comprehensive reforms for future advocacy campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The timeline notes agreements requiring Fluent, Opt-Intelligence, and React2Media to 'adopt comprehensive reforms in future advocacy campaigns and pay more than $4.4 million in penalties and disgorgement.' Later actions secured additional penalties. Guidance: civil penalties and injunctive remedies are appropriate enforcement tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-agency awareness and investigation of similar comment fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Because mass comment fraud may affect multiple agencies, federal oversight and law enforcement should examine similar patterns across agencies and not treat incidents as isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House Democrats wrote that 'It now appears that the fake comments submitted to the FCC … were not an isolated incident' and cited similar fraud at CFPB, DOL, FERC and SEC. Guidance: multi-agency coordination is necessary to detect and deter widespread abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of oversight mechanisms (GAO, state AGs, lawsuits) to examine agency conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies are uncooperative or suspected of withholding information, oversight bodies (GAO, state attorneys general) and suit for judicial review are appropriate means to investigate agency conduct and the integrity of rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: House Democrats called on GAO to investigate; NY AG repeatedly requested logs and issued subpoenas; Jason Prechtel sued the FCC for FOIA noncompliance; Free Press filed suit in appeals court citing 'fraudulent submissions that the FCC refused to investigate.' Guidance: pursue oversight and legal remedies where necessary.
